This section examines Experiment J —
Pre-flight diagnostics from first

principles. Keep two questions separate:
does changing the order change

the measured outcome, and does the
proposed search method beat

a matched alternative at the same
distinct-evaluation budget? Teach both
statistics before showing the outcome:

rho_1=operatorname{corr}(f(pi),f(m(pi)))
where m is one mutation move, and F

D C correlates fitness with distance to
the nearest optimum.

Setup: about 4,000 sampled moves in the
initial study across

eight enumerated landscapes; later
sampling audit used 100 pairs per

operator and 200 F D C points, repeated
200 times.

Operator recovery: Hamming→swap
rho_1=0.655; Kendall→insert 0.777;

adjacency→inversion 0.675. Regime
separation: strongly negative F D C

accompanied fast convergence; parity n=7
was about −0.06 and behaved

like random; deceptive fitness had F D C
about +0.78

despite smoothness near 0.65. Sampling
audit: correct typed-landscape

operator selected about 94–99% of the
time. Caveat: scramble identity

moves can inflate its autocorrelation;
exclude it from a naïve

argmax. Visual: two landscapes with the
same smooth local appearance

but opposite F D C guidance. Now read
evidence panel

J-locality. The axes, units, and sample
are stated on screen.

The sample represented here is the sample
reported in the

source. Raw observations remain visible
wherever the artifact provides them.

Censored observations stay marked at the
cap rather than becoming

invented hitting times, and sampled
landscapes leave unobserved permutations

blank. The supported finding is: Teach

the outcome:
rho_1=operatorname{corr}(f(pi),f(m(pi)))

mutation move, and F D C correlates
fitness with distance

to the nearest optimum. The broader claim
not established here

is: Caveat: scramble identity moves can
inflate its autocorrelation; exclude

it from a naïve argmax. This evidence
changed the program

as follows: Carry this constraint into the
next experiment and

compare methods at equal cost. The
distinction is part of

the result. A large ordering effect does
not automatically imply

an evolutionary-search advantage, and
almost-sure convergence does not
promise practical efficiency.
